newsitem.title: GERMANY: Rift widens between Kohl's CDU and CSU over euro.
newsitem.headline: Rift widens between Kohl's CDU and CSU over euro.

text.p: A row between Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Bavarian sister party the Christian Social Union (CSU) flared on Sunday over how strictly to assess the finances of states wanting to launch Europe's single currency.

European Union states wanting to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) must post a maximum budget deficit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) as set down in the Maastricht Treaty on EMU.

But since the election of France's new left-wing government, a rift has widened between the CDU and CSU, a core part of Kohl's ruling coalition, over whether this means exactly 3.0 percent or just a shade more.
Fearing Paris will seek to dilute the EMU criteria, the CSU has made it clear it would prefer to see Europe's single currency delayed rather than risk it being weak.

Kohl's powerful lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble told MDR radio he was confident Germany would pass the financial test to qualify for launching Europe's planned single currency, the euro, and argued three percent did not have to mean 3.0.

"Germany will fulfil the criteria to qualify for the euro. The figures after the decimal point are important but not decisive," Schaueble, CDU/CSU parliamentary group leader in Bonn, said in an interview.
"The essential thing is to set the course for undoubted lasting stability of the European currency," he said.
Kohl, speaking at a Group of Seven (G7) summit in Denver, United States, stood on his insistence that the euro would arrive on time. But he omitted to say how strictly it would fulfil the criteria.
"I have never doubted this...My (G7) colleagues are in absolutely no doubt about this," Kohl told ZDF's Bonn Direkt programme, according to a transcript of the interview released in Bonn.

Bavarian finance minister Erwin Huber, who is a close political ally of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, told the Berliner Morgenpost newspaper on Saturday EMU should not go ahead unless participants strictly met the Maastricht criteria.
This, Huber said, was a chief guarantee of stability for the planned euro, which most Germans, according to opinion polls, fear will be softer than their beloved mark.
Huber said it would not be enough for Germany to meet the three percent ratio of deficit to GDP reference target stated in the Maastricht Treaty if other countries were to overshoot it, he said.
"From our point of view, that means that France must reach three in the sense of 3.0," Huber was quoted as saying.

German newspapers reported that Kohl had criticised the CSU in Bavaria during last week's European Union summit in Amsterdam for their "unusally foolish talk" of keeping to the 3.0 interpretation of the criteria.

Edmund Stoiber, the powerful CSU premier of the southern state of Bavaria, said Kohl had criticised another leading CSU figure there on the edge of the EU summit, Kurt Faltlhauser, for brewing trouble for EMU.
But Stoiber told Welt am Sonntag newspaper Kohl had not criticised the Bavarian government or himself over their tough EMU stance.

Stoiber said he failed to comprehend such criticism because Kohl's CDU relied on the CSU for its 12-seat majority in the Bundestag lower house of parliament in Bonn and would not be in power without the Bavarian party.
